The 2025 season provided ideal outcomes for fantasy managers who invested in elite starting pitchers. That season, Tarik Skubal, Paul Skenes, Garrett Crochet and Zack Wheeler were the top four pitchers drafted. Per our Fantasy Player Rater, Skubal ($35.5), Crochet ($32.8) and Skenes ($30.8) finished 1-2-3 among starting pitchers in all roto formats. Wheeler finished 14th ($22.6) despite his season being cut short. As is the case every single year, to varying degrees, there were mid-round arms who produced elite roto seasons (Bryan Woo, Hunter Brown, Max Fried), as well starters such as Nathan Eovaldi, Matthew Boyd, and Trevor Rogers who provided hefty profit a as late-round picks and free agent acquisitions.
As is also the case every season, there were early-round landmines. Cole Ragans, Blake Snell, and Corbin Burnes all missed at least two-thirds of the season due to injuries. Logan Gilbert investors certainly weren’t thrilled about his abbreviated season with only six wins. Nevertheless, dream seasons from the Crème de la crème instilled an illusion of tranquility at the top of the SP pool for 2026 drafts despite the position’s inherent risks and volatile history.
The calm ominously turned to storm on Opening Day. Paul Skenes couldn’t get out of the first inning against the Mets, allowing five earned runs, as droves of social media melodramatics scolded us: “…and that’s why you never draft pitchers early!” Skenes (174 IP – 200 K – 10 W – 3.82 – 1.12) inevitably lost “fantasy god” status as his price dropped a couple of rounds for 2027 drafts. Skubal was a top 10 pitcher with elite ratios, but did not have his usual season of dominance due to missing 5-6 starts. Crochet was an injury landmine and one of many early-round busts.
There were some wins in the second tier (Yoshinobu Yamamoto, Chris Sale) as well as disappointments (Bryan Woo, Hunter Brown, Ragans again), but what may be most memorable about last season’s starting pitcher pool was that leagues were won without having to invest in early starting pitchers at all. Of course, that only happened to managers who side-stepped the early-round hitter landmines like Aaron Judge, Ronald Acuña Jr., Vladimir Guerrero Jr., Francisco Lindor and Cal Raleigh. The two top producers – Jacob Misiorowski and Cam Schlittler – were post-100 ADP picks. Of the 19 starters who earned $14 or more in 12-team leagues, 13 had an ADP of 100+, including six with an ADP of 250 or greater.

These are the pitchers with ADPs in the first five rounds of OCs. Ohtani could technically be excluded since he was mostly used as a hitter in NFBC formats last season. He did earn nearly $14, producing sparkling ratios (1.79 ERA, 0.95 WHIP) with 95 strikeouts in 85.2 innings (14 starts). Ohtani should pitch again next season, but will be a top-three consensus fantasy pick regardless. No matter where he signs, Skubal will be the first or second SP off draft boards, along with Misiorowski. Sale, Yamamoto and Cristopher Sánchez will likely live in the Round 2 range. Sale was the SP3 in 2024, SP20 in 2025 and SP4 in 2026. Yamamoto was the SP7 and SP3 in his first two full Major League seasons. Sánchez has posted consecutive seasons of 200+ innings and a sub-3.00 ERA. Hunter Brown will be a polarizing pick in the Rounds 4-7 range coming off a 20-start season where he produced a strong 3.19 ERA, but saw his WHIP and walk rate balloon from the previous season — from 1.03 and 7.8% to 1.27 and 12.2%.
A fantasy bust in 2026, Freddy Peralta is quickly surging back up confidence meters and draft boards with his dominant playoff performances. Bryan Woo and Logan Gilbert will be slightly discounted coming off disappointing seasons, but T-Mobile Park in Seattle remains advantageous to starting pitchers (30-of-30 in MLB Park Factor for hits in 2026) and bounce-backs wouldn’t be shocking, assuming good health. Ragans underwent UCL repair surgery in July and has a 10-12 month return timetable, so he’s off our radars for the forseeable future. Jacob deGrom was slightly more human in his age-38 season, posting a career-worst 4.20 ERA, albeit with a 3.11 FIP, 3.14 xFIP and 3.15 SIERA.
Fried’s UCL is “in a good place” according to NY Daily News writer, Gary Phillips. Logan Webb is no longer the position’s Iron Man and could fall out of the top 100 ADP, though he will always have supporters. A healthy Webb could provide profit at a reasonable cost.

The 61-120 ADP range was quite the mixed bag.
Dylan Cease and Jesús Luzardo were studs and will be drafted in the top 50 in most formats.
Wheeler recovered thoroughly from his thoracic outlet procedure and produced yet another $20+ season: 162 IP (28 starts) – 193 K – 14 W – 3.00 – 1.05. He has been the best pitcher in the Majors since 2021, leading in wins (79), ERA (2.92) and second in strikeouts (1,234) behind Cease’s 1,345.
Chase Burns will be highly coveted after his masterful performance over his first full season (154.1 IP – 185 K – 15 W – 2.86 – 1.17) and will be drafted among the top 12 to 15 starters. Nolan McLean will be slightly cheaper than Burns after his first full and successful season in the Majors. Cases made against either this offseason will start with concerns about their lack of elite control and potential WHIP damage at Tier 2 SP prices. Eury Pérez is in this boat as well after posting a 10.3% walk rate and a 1.21 WHIP, though don’t expect to pay anything but a premium for the coveted fireballer who will turn 24 in April.
Joe Ryan should be a solid pick among the top 100 as well. Though he may never have that 180+ IP dream season where good health and all the cards align, Ryan has been a dependable fantasy stud, posting a K-BB% over 20% for four straight seasons and has made between 23 and 30 starts over his first five full seasons.
There were quite a few negative value guys in this range, which was quite shocking for some: George Kirby, Kyle Bradish, Framber Valdez, Kevin Gausman and Emmet Sheehan. Kirby is quickly becoming persona non grata in the fantasy community, posting a painful 1.40 WHIP last season and two straight years with a 4.00+ ERA. Bradish’s WHIP (1.42) was even worse than Kirby’s as he did most of his damage after the All-Star break, posting a 5.29 ERA and a .398 wOBA in those final 10 starts before getting shelved due to lower abdominal pain and being diagnosed with a sports hernia. Gausman compiled 30+ starts for a sixth consecutive season. Despite nearly all of his rate stats and underlying metrics matching last season’s, Gausman posted a 4.51 ERA, with an xFIP and SIERA over a full run lower. I’ll remind myself of how solid everything looked under the hood for Gausman and would consider targeting him again in 2027 drafts. Sheehan isn’t going to fly under the radar this draft season despite last year’s poor results. The key here, of course, is Sheehan having a rotation spot. He dominated in his time down in Triple-A and fired three gems for the Dodgers in September (0.53 ERA, 24:3 K:BB in 17 innings/3 starts).

The 120-180 ADP range was Landmine Central — pitchers like Castillo, Imai, and Chandler decimated our ratios. There were likely some folks who were duped for another round of category destruction when Castillo joined the White Sox. Castillo’s 5.85 ERA was third-worst among the 94 pitchers who threw at least 130 innings. The only ones worse were Kyle Freeland (6.65) and Jeffrey Springs (6.18). At least both of them had bad home parks as an excuse.
Rasmussen and Gray sported matching 2.72 ERAs and finished as top 12 starters. Both will be highly coveted by drafters and I’m sure that the Rasmussen helium will take soar him into the third round of 12-teamers, especially with the glow of playoff glory. Gray dazzled with a below-average strikeout rate of 21.8%, which was 6-7% lower than his two previous seasons in St. Louis. Because of some peripheral drop-offs and his age (36), don’t be surprised to see Gray fall into some offseason bust articles.
Imanaga had three massive disaster starts in the second half of May, but his overall production was strong and his control is on the border of elite. He posted a 5.2% walk rate and a 24.6% strikeout rate and owns a 19.4% K-BB% over three Major League seasons. He’s a free agent who the Cubs would love to re-sign, though we should expect the Padres to show strong interest. I’m definitely interested in Imanaga next season.
Robbie Ray is also a free agent who should generate offseason interest. He will certainly experience a price dip from the 100s to the 200s after a visit from the control boogie man (12% BB) last season.
Gavin Williams led the AL in strikeouts, fueled by an impressive 15% swinging-strike rate. More importantly, he reduced a near-12% walk rate down to below nine percent last season. Williams won’t be cheap in drafts, and rightfully so.

There were some stretches of fantasy usefulness from several in this tier, but no big payoffs. Ryan Weathers’ first season in the AL was a roller coaster ride, but mostly positive. He finished the season with a 3.60 ERA aligned with peripherals (3.50 SIERA, 3.44 xFIP), a 1.22 WHIP, and a 18.5% K-BB%. His roto value was weighed down by just five victories. Carlos Rodón was a properly discounted stash who was activated on May 10 and pitched nine starts before elbow inflammation reappeared and he missed two months of the summer. The end-of-season line was good (2.67 ERA, 1.06 WHIP, 26.8% K in 16 starts). His 11.2% walk rate wasn’t and it was his first season over 10% in the post-Covid era. An air of trepidation will likely always remain for Rodón because of his elbow, which may result in a 2027 discount, with profitability a likely outcome if his UCL stays intact.
Jack Flaherty and Zac Gallen are falling semi-stars who were unmitigated disasters last season. Gallen finished with a 3-9 record and a 6.07 ERA in 105.1 innings. Flaherty threw just 88.1 innings and had a 4.48 ERA with his typical high strikeout rate (26%). Flaherty and Gallen are both free agents. They’ll be more appealing to real-life teams than to fantasy managers.
Tanner Bibee makes 30 starts a season, but is essentially just a thrower now. He has posted an ERA over 4.00 for a second straight season and has seen his strikeout rate reduced in three consecutive seasons — from 26.3% to 21.3% to 19%. Bibee has three years left on his 5yr, $45M deal.
Trey Yesavage was certainly trending toward Miz and Schlittler range this winter and early spring, earning a minimum pick of 113 in Online Championships. Yesavage ADP helium was quickly popped a week before Opening Day because of right shoulder impingement. In the Too Early Meatball draft in August, Yesavage was drafted in the 15th round, and this is a 15-team format. It would hard to imagine Yesavage not rising up boards back into the top 150 overall. He has a spot in the Jays rotation so all he needs know is to stay healthy.

A long list of names, so we’ll just touch on a few of them. Among the studs who provided tremendous profit were Cade Cavalli, Reid Detmers, Nick Martinez, Payton Tolle, and the impenetrable Eduardo Rodriguez, who pulled off 17 wins with a 2.89 ERA despite a much higher xFIP (4.44) and SIERA (4.62) and the lowest BABIP (.274 of his career). I don’t usually mess with the peripheral gods and will stubbornly skip over him in early drafts. Cade Cavalli had an epic run after the All-Star break, posting a 90:16 K:BB and a 1.90 ERA over his final 12 starts. Reid Detmers was having a decent season, but really began to shine when the Angels fired pitching coach Mike Maddux. Over those final 8 starts, Detmers posted a 4-0 record with a 1.62 ERA and an impressive 55:5 K:BB. Angels fans are hoping that the new regime under new owner Stan Kroenke will bring the organization from the basement to at least the living room. Interim GM John Mozeliak will stay in the role for now and help the Angels find a permanent GM and a new manager, since Kurt Suzuki is one-and-done.
A $1.20 earning shouldn’t detract from the admiration that Clay Holmes should receive after Round 15 in 12-teamers. He produced a respectable 3.29 ERA, but his low value was impacted by a low strikeout rate (18.6%), six wins, and time spent on the IL, which led to just 18 starts on the season. Michael Wacha was stellar yet again, earning $10 in 12-team NFBC roto leagues as the SP29. Taj Bradley, Troy Melton, Ian Seymour, Justin Wrobleski, and Michael Soroka all had some strong stretches of production that helped fantasy managers, especially those who got out of the Wrobleski business before that ship began to sank. Seymour and Melton are already earning some early 2027 draft love, getting scooped up among the top 50 starters in the 150-175 ADP range — a price that is likely to surge as we move through the heart of draft season.
Finally, a shout out to FAAB stud Sean Burke who broke out in a big way. He produced a 3.34 ERA, a 1.20 WHIP and punched out 185 batters over 172.1 innings. Burke had a scorching-hot nine-start run from June 18 through August 11 where he rocked a 1.60 ERA and struck out 79, with just 11 walks over 62 innings. He had some rough starts, but was still worth every free agent penny. Based on some of the prices (2-5% of budget), it almost felt like pennies were what were being spent.
It’s always a good idea to dig into player stats not long after the season has ended. It helps avoid building biases that may fester, resonate, and solidify within our draft tendencies for the coming draft season. When we wait too long into the winter to review individual player profiles, we increase the likelihood of outside influences manipulating our valuations of players — whether it’s articles that do a good job of convincing a player is a boon or a bust, social media bandwaggoning, or ADP data itself. We don’t have to decide between Ashcraft and McLean now, but if we’re equipped with the details of their stats, underlying metrics, velocity trends, pitch mix changes, Stuff, and healthy history, we can limit emotion and bias from our decision-making and make optimal, objective decisions during the heart of draft season.

item.content:encoded:
The World Series is about to begin, and we’re being treated to a doozy of a series between the Brewers and the Rays. However, for the 28 other teams, they are turning their attention to 2027, so we’ll join them in that for a bit with some starting pitcher rankings for next season.
This is now my fourth year publishing my starting pitcher rankings and my second year doing it this early. In many ways, I like doing a first pass at rankings this year. At this point, it’s hard to overthink. Most players aren’t playing games or posting videos of new pitches, so there is nothing to get geeked about. Instead, these rankings are more “gut feel” rankings based on how I feel about all of these pitchers at the end of the season. While I tried not to get too in the weeds about stats, I did look back at the general profile that allowed a pitcher to finish among the top 30 overall starters in recent years, and tried to prioritize pitchers who fit that profile, which mostly meant elevating pitchers who get swings and misses, and penalizing pitchers who don’t seem like a good bet for a full season of innings.
As always, the pitchers are split into tiers based on their skillset or what they’ll provide your fantasy team. The tiers themselves are more important than the rankings inside the tiers, so I wouldn’t split hairs over a few spots in the rankings. I’ve also ranked these pitchers as if I’m doing a 12-team league, so safe but boring low-end starters take a hit in value, etc. I won’t have really long write-ups here, but I’ll be back with updated rankings after the new year, where we can get a little more into the nitty-gritty of the rankings.

item.content:encoded:
Tarik Skubal and the Los Angeles Dodgers were swept out of the NLCS by the 103-win Milwaukee Brewers, a refreshing change of pace after two years of Dodgers dominance — and a helpful reminder to the MLB owners that payroll alone does not determine winning. It also leaves Skubal with a more difficult decision in free agency than many expected.
The Dodgers will not re-sign Skubal before the lockout in December, as there's simply too much risk without knowing how the salary cap will function come 2027. Really regardless of how MLB's labor dispute plays out, however, Los Angeles will hope to retain Skubal, who is still rightly regarded as the most bankable ace in baseball. The question is: Are the Dodgers the favorites for his services? Let's rank all realistic suitors, from least to most realistic.
8. Philadelphia Phillies
The Phillies are desperate and the Phillies typically spend money. Not necessarily as liberally as fans would like, but it's not impossible to imagine Dave Dombrowski — with the World Series window closing rapidly on this aging core — deciding that Skubal is worth an all-in push.
It would give Philadelphia the most talented rotation in MLB between Skubal, Zack Wheeler, Cristopher Sánchez, Jesús Luzardo and Aaron Nola, four of whom could compete for NL Cy Young next season. There's also Andrew Painter, a former top prospect who came into his own down the stretch and delivered big outs in the postseason, to provide depth.
The Phillies probably have enough money wrapped up in that rotation (and in Bryce Harper, Kyle Schwarber and Trea Turner) to be turned off of paying Skubal top dollar, but it's a fun thought for a team hoping to lean even more on run prevention moving forward.
7. Boston Red Sox
The Red Sox wielded one of the deepest and most reliable rotations in MLB last season; that was with top ace Garrett Crochet on the IL. Upon Crochet's return, Boston will have a compelling blend of experience (Crochet, Ranger Suárez) and emerging youth (Payton Tolle, Jake Bennett) to throw at their opponents.
Then again, they know the toll injuries can take, and Sonny Gray — probably their best regular season starter this past season — is now a free agent. The Red Sox could simply line up a new contract for Gray and be content, but why not aim higher? Skubal has proven remarkably durable over the years and he offers Boston a much longer window as Crochet's partner in crime. Suddenly, the Red Sox have the best one-two punch in baseball and it wouldn't be especially close.
After the Yankees lit them up in the Wild Card round (and after Boston's top arms couldn't pitch deep into either postseason game), there's pressure for a big swing.
6. Chicago Cubs
There's no doubting the Cubs' ability to generate offense, but the rotation has been a sore spot for years now. Jed Hoyer has shown a great appetite for spending in free agency of late; the Alex Bregman signing was a real flex. That said, Chicago needs to allocate more resources toward pitching. The Edward Cabrera trade went belly up. Shōta Imanaga is a free agent now, as are trade deadline pickups Kevin Gausman and Clay Holmes.
Chicago will get help internally with both Cade Horton and Justin Steele returning from season-long elbow injuries; Ben Brown, who finally broke out in 2026, should also be back in the mix. Beyond them, however, it's pretty grim. Matthew Boyd and Javier Assad can eat innings in the regular season, but neither has proven able to pitch deep in October — at least not consistently.
Skubal would deliver Chicago the frontline ace it has long lacked, with a solid scaffolding of talent behind him. The Cubs would be much better positioned to challenge Milwaukee in the division and potentially emerge from a crowded National League field.
5. Detroit Tigers
Skubal has made it clear he would've spent his entire career in Detroit if it was up to him. All the Tigers need to do is come through with a competitive offer. While last year's surprise Framber Valdez signing was a positive indication of the front office's competitive intent, there's a reason no Skubal extension ever came to fruition — or even remotely close.
A client of Scott Boras, Skubal was never inclined to sign an extension. But the Tigers' offers weren't even in the parking lot, much less the ballpark. Detroit will need to scale up its ambition significantly if it wants to lure Skubal back to the midwest.
All that said, Skubal has an affection for Detroit that's worth mentioning. The Tigers also desperately need a frontline ace in Skubal's mold. Young bucks like Troy Melton, Keider Montero, Jackson Jobe and River Ryan are very talented, but the Tigers don't really have an established vet besides Valdez, who was a mess last season.
4. New York Yankees
The Yankees tend to flex their muscles in free agency, although with diminishing returns in recent years. New York is no longer the most lucrative destination for a lot of A-tier stars. Juan Soto a couple years ago, Kyle Tucker last winter; the Yankees are getting outbid pretty consistently these days. That has not stopped New York from stockpiling stars, though, especially in the rotation.
It would require Hal Steinbrenner and the front office to basically sign off on a blank check, but the Yankees' ALDS loss to the Rays was a sobering defeat. There are cracks in the foundation. Many of those cracks are injury-related and concentrated in the lineup; Cam Schlittler, Max Fried, Gerrit Cole and Carlos Rodón is as strong a four-man gauntlet as any rotation in MLB. The Yankees also have Ryan Weathers, Will Warren and top prospects like Elmer Rodríguez and Carlos Lagrange for depth.
Still, the Yankees know the importance of depth, especially as their non-Schlittler core ages and becomes more injury-prone. Skubal provides stability and instantly lends credibility to any postseason aspirations. Schlittler-Skubal becomes the most fearsome pitching duo in baseball. Never say never.
3. Toronto Blue Jays
The Blue Jays have steadily become the most aggressive front office in the American League. After finishing runner-up in the Juan Soto and Shohei Ohtani sweepstakes, Toronto extended Vladimir Guerrero Jr. at a $500 million price point and signed Dylan Cease in the early days of free agency last winter. A disappointing season should not preclude Toronto from maintaining its all-in approach; if anything, it's more motivation for the Blue Jays to stack talent. This team was in the World Series a year ago.
Toronto is a great market, with a vibrant local culture and an entire country behind the Blue Jays. That ought to appeal to the vanity of a star like Skubal, who would team up with the projected AL Cy Young runner-up in Cease. The Jays also made a savvy trade for José Soriano at the deadline, adding another premium arm in his prime. Trey Yesavage, once healthy, could resume his ascent to stardom. The talent is there.
Skubal solidifies Toronto as a legitimate World Series contender coming into 2027. Moreover, the Jays have a lot of money coming off the books, which should free up the front office to spend recklessly where it counts. Toronto is always the "dark horse" in these top-dollar bidding wars, but ruling out the Blue Jays would be foolish.
2. Los Angeles Dodgers
It's impossible to rule out the incumbents. Los Angeles made the Skubal trade in part because of their deep farm system — and in part because it set the stage for a potential long-term partnership. There's a reason small-market front offices were unwilling to match L.A.'s outgoing package (see: Brewers). The Dodgers could afford to trade two of the 50ish best prospects in baseball because the team can feel reasonably good about both competing for a World Series this season (oh well) and re-signing Skubal when he hits the open market.
An NLCS loss does complicate the situation somewhat, not to mention the unknowability of upcoming labor disputes. The Dodgers' loss was a direct result of investing hundreds of millions of dollars in stars who are beginning to decline. Mookie Betts, Freddie Freeman, Shohei Ohtani, Will Smith, Tyler Glasnow and Blake Snell are all on the wrong side of 30; Tucker will join that list next season. Los Angeles will endure more and more diminishing returns.
That said, nothing (besides a strict salary cap) can really stop the Dodgers from compensating for declining stars by signing more expensive stars, even if it leaves the cap sheet in utter chaos five years from now. That has been L.A.'s strategy to date; it was part of the logic behind the Skubal trade. The Dodgers still arguably represent Skubal's best chance to win a World Series, which will no doubt be part of the calculus if another team can't dramatically outspend them.
1. New York Mets
If any team can blow L.A.'s offer out of the water, it's the Mets. Steve Cohen is baseball's richest owner and New York has consistently tossed its hat in the ring for MLB's premium free agents. Juan Soto's $765 million contract set a new record; Skubal very well could set a record for pitchers.
The Mets are coming off of a last-place season, too, which only fuels anxiety in the fan base. It should also fuel aggression in the front office. David Stearns is under pressure to prove that he has what it takes to win in New York. Skubal would join an emerging ace in Nolan McLean, plus other whippersnappers like Zac Thornton and Jonah Tong. The Mets need depth besides, as Kodai Senga and Sean Manaea look more like bullpen arms these days. New York, however, is the one non-Dodgers team with enough money to sign Skubal and pursue other targets.
If the Dodgers get spooked by the shadow of their own payroll, which is more likely than ever, the Mets are the logical team we can expect to swoop in and win the Skubal bidding war outright.

item.content:encoded:
The offseason is a perfect time for New York Mets fans like myself to be optimistic, and that's exactly what I'm going to be doing here when I say the stars are aligning for the Mets to sign Tarik Skubal in free agency. I know, this seems crazy. Why would Skubal want to join a Mets team that just won 74 games in 2026 and has failed to make the playoffs in each of Juan Soto's two years in Flushing?
Well, here's a look at why the Mets make more sense for Skubal than you might think, and what might stand in their way of making this dream of arguably the best pitcher in the sport playing out the rest of his prime in Queens a reality.
The Dodgers' lack of aggression might play into the Mets' hands
When the Los Angeles Dodgers traded for Tarik Skubal, MLB fans not only assumed they'd automatically win a World Series title, but they also assumed that the Dodgers would easily extend Skubal, given their recent history of spending on star-level talent. It's absolutely possible that the Dodgers do choose to re-sign Skubal, but look at what ESPN's Alden Gonzalez had to say about that.
"Skubal's agent, Scott Boras, will probably want to get something done with his client before the lockout, but it would be really difficult for the Dodgers to justify signing Skubal to a massive deal before knowing what MLB's economic model will look like," Gonzalez wrote. "If there is a cap-and-floor system in the next collective bargaining agreement, there will be some sort of phase-in period. But it will undoubtedly impact the Dodgers in the near future. It would be a major risk to sign Skubal before knowing what they're signing up for."
To sum up, Gonzalez is predicting that Skubal's agent, Scott Boras, will likely want to get a deal done with his top client before the expected lockout at the beginning of December, but the Dodgers would want to wait until after the lockout so they know what the economic model of the sport will look like. This makes a ton of sense, given the massive amount of money they've already committed to 2027 and beyond. It's worth noting that this is just Gonzalez's belief, and not a sourced report.
If the Dodgers won't aggressively pursue Skubal before December 1, why can't the Mets be the team to give him an offer he can't refuse? It's not like the Mets haven't been in this position before.
The Mets have beaten the competition to the punch pre-lockout before
Just like a lockout is looming this offseason, one loomed back in the 2021 offseason, when Max Scherzer was a free agent. Scherzer, who was represented by Scott Boras, made it clear that he wanted to sign before the league locked the players out, and he did just that, coming to terms on a three-year, $130 milllion deal with, guess who, the New York Mets.
Now, say what you want about how the deal aged (Scherzer pitched brilliantly in 2022 but struggled in that year's postseason and was traded at the 2023 trade deadline), but the Mets beat the Dodgers and a couple of other teams to the punch to sign the future Hall of Famer on a deal that paid him well over $40 million annually.
Can't that history repeat itself? The Mets won the Scherzer sweepstakes not because they were some powerhouse, but because the Dodgers didn't want to go above and beyond to sign him as the Mets did. Reports suggest Skubal would like to sign pre-lockout and the Dodgers don't want to go above and beyond. Why can't the Mets do what they've already done and give their fan base something to get excited about before the lockout?
If the Dodgers and Mets won't pay Tarik Skubal, what team will?
Let's just assume that both the Dodgers and the Mets decide that paying Skubal is not in their best interest. Is there another team out there willing to spend the $300-to-$400 million on Skubal that he'll likely be asking for?
The New York Yankees are often willing spenders, but with a ton of money invested in starting pitchers like Gerrit Cole, Max Fried and Carlos Rodon, would they pay Skubal before addressing their offense? The Philadelphia Phillies should be eager to spend after another early elimination, but again, is paying on pitching in their best interest? The Chicago Cubs could certainly use the pitching, but they've never even handed out a $200 million contract. Would they give $300+ million to Skubal? The Toronto Blue Jays have the money and the need for pitching help, but they also just paid Dylan Cease handsomely last winter and finished last in runs scored this past season. A return to the Detroit Tigers would be awesome, but that feels unrealistic.
There're other teams like the San Francisco Giants and the Los Angeles Angels who might show interest, but again, there isn't really a perfect fit. If the Mets and Dodgers won't meet an outlandish asking price, which team will?
The Mets have a clear need for a high-end starting pitcher
The Mets are building a strong rotation, with youngsters like Nolan McLean, Christian Scott and Zac Thornton in the fold, but the team lacks a true ace. They hoped Freddy Peralta would fill that void when they acquired him from the Brewers in the 2025 offseason, but that experiment flopped spectacularly.
It's hard to see Skubal flopping, though, at least in 2027. He remains one of, if not the best pitcher in the sport, and even after an early-season injury scare, Skubal ended his season with a 2.72 ERA in 26 starts. He's as dynamic as they come, and would instantly make the Mets true postseason contenders.
If they don't sign Skubal, who else could they realistically get? The next-best options, such as Michael King, Kevin Gausman and Clay Holmes, aren't exactly aces. They could potentially swing a trade, but doing so is easier said than done. It feels like Skubal or bust when it comes to getting a bona fide ace.
Would David Stearns be willing to abandon his starting pitching philosophy to sign Tarik Skubal?
We know that the Mets have the need, the money and the location necessary to lure Skubal to the team, but would the individual responsible for making such a move, David Stearns, be willing to do so? Stearns has famously been averse to handing massive deals to starting pitchers, passing on guys like Corbin Burnes, Max Fried and Dylan Cease, to name a few, and instead relying on shorter-term gambles.
Most of these have not paid off, which is partially why the Mets have missed the playoffs in back-to-back years, but will there be a mindset shift? Will Stearns suddenly go from a guy unwilling to offer more than three years to a pitcher over the age of 30 to willing to meet Skubal's demands?
That's an answer we're soon going to learn the answer to, and it could be the difference in Skubal joining the Mets or signing elsewhere. If Stearns is all in, the stars feel like they're aligning for something special to happen.

2026 was the final season of Kevin Gausman's five-year, $110 million free-agent contract. In the first four seasons, Kevin posted a 48-41 record, a 3.48 ERA, and an 11.5 bWAR. A good return on a big free-agent contract. Not all that many of those go as well as this one did.
But 2026 was his age-35 season, and sometimes pitchers don't do well in their mid-30s.

Baseball Reference has him at a 1.1 WAR (down from 4.0). FanGraphs 3.1 (down from 4.1), giving him a value of $25.1 million to the Jays and Cubs.
He had a 3.3.74 FIP and a 3.58 xFIP, which is why the FanGraphs WAR is so much better than the Baseball Reference one.
Kevin's BABIP was .311 (up from.262 last year). 68.7% of his base runner were stranded (down from 72.2%).
His line drive rate was down a little bit (19.6% from 21.3 last year), ground ball rate up (40.3% down from 36.7), and fly ball rate much the same (40.3% from 42.0). 12.7% of fly balls hit off him left the park, up from 9.5.
His strikeout rate about the same (24.5% from 24.4), and his walk rate was down a bit (6.3% from 6.5).
Kevin's soft contact was up (17.4% from 15.1 last year) and hard contact about the same (35.9% from 36.2).
He was better against LHB (.251/.304/.389) than RHB (.269/.307/.459). He's been slightly better against LHB for his career.
He was better at home (3.83 ERA, batters hit .264/.299/.439) than on the road (5.40, .253/.313/.394).
Kevin was better in the first half of the season (4.33, .244/.296/.405) than the second half (4.82, .284/.320/.444).
Gausman by month:
- April: 7 starts, 2-2, 3.10. Batters hit .204/.244/.349, 5 home runs, 8 walks and 40 strikeouts.
- May: 5 starts, 2-1, 3.18. Batters hit .291/.316/.364, 1 home run, 4 walks and 26 strikeouts.
- June: 6 starts, 0-4, 6.47. Batters hit .262/.324/.556, 9 home runs, 12 walks and 34 strikeouts.
- July: 4 starts, 0-3, 6.10. Batters hit .280/.366/.317, 3 home runs, 11 walks and 23 strikeouts.
- August: 6 starts, 4-1, 4.54. Batters hit .275/.312/.443, 5 home runs, 8 walks and 33 strikeouts.
- September: 4 starts, 1-1, 4.43. Batters hit .267/.298/.478, 6 home runs, 4 walks and 28 strikeouts.
The Jays were 9-14 in his starts. The Cubs were 5-4 in his starts. Between the two teams, they averaged 4.05 runs scored in games he started. They scored 2 or less runs in 13 of his starts.
Days of rest:
- 4 days, 12 games: 3.54, .246/.288/.404.
- 5 days, 16 games: 5.26, .265/.313/.433.
- 6 or more days, 4 games: 4.50, .275/.326/.413
I love guys who are best on normal rest. I think we are all creatures of habit, you get in a routine and things go well, you leave that routine and they don't got as well. He was also best on normal rest last year.
Times through the order:
- 1st: Batters hit .233/.276/.346.
- 2nd: Batters hit .270/.318/.460.
- 3rd: Batters hit .286/.333/.478.
- And he faced 1 batter a fourth time, getting the out.
I wonder if he would consider being a reliever next year? That might be reading too much into one season, in 2025 he was pretty much the same for each of the first three times through the order.

- Brandon Valenzuela: 4.46, .254/.298/.396 in 308 PA.
- Alejandro Kirk: 4.81, .263/.324/.419 in 185 PA.
- Carson Kelly: 4.20, .226/.268/.426 in 123 PA.
- Miguel Amaya: 5.75, .305/.333/.500 in 87 PA.
- Tyler Heineman: 2.31, .273/.319/.409 in 47 PA.
Kevin's best start, by GameScore, was a 78 on April 1st, at home against the Rockies. He went 6 innings, 2 hits, 0 earned runs, 0 walks, and 10 strikeouts. He also had a 77 and two 76s.
Worst start? A 13 in Chicago against the Cubs, on June 19th. You likely remember it: 2 innings, 7 hits, 7 earned runs, 1 home run, 4 walks and 3 strikeouts. We used six relievers, two days after a bullpen day, and the next day Patrick Corbin was pulled after 3.2 innings.
Kevin averaged 5.5 innings per start in his 23 starts with us. And about the same in his 9 starts with the Cubs. His one playoff start didn't go all that well: 3.1 innings, 3 earned.
He threw, for the most part, three pitches:
- Four Seamer: 93.8 mph (last year it averaged 94.5). Batters hit .289 against it (.230 last year).
- Split finger: 84 mph (last year it averaged 94.9). Batters hit .207 against it (.191 last year).
- Slider: 84.1 mph (last year it averaged 83.2). Batters hit .324 against it (.333 last year).
Random Baseball Savant numbers:
- Fastball Run Value: 87th percentile.
- Breaking Ball Run Value: 7th percentile.
- Chase Rate: 88th percentile.
- Strikeout %: 70th percentile.
- Walk %: 86th percentile.
- Barrell %: 46th percentile.
- Hard Hit %: 34th percentile.
- Expected ERA: 53rd percentile.
With the Jays, he posted a 53-51 record and a 3.63 ERA, with a 12.5 bWAR (and a 21 fWAR). FanGraphs says he was worth $167.6 million over his five-year contract, and he was paid $110 million, so we got more than our money's worth.
On the Jays career leaderboard:
- 11th in pitcher bWAR: 12.5.
- 7th in ERA: 3.62
- 11th in wins: 53 (tied with Jose Berrios)
- 11th in innings pitched: 861.0.
- 7th in strikeouts: 920.
- 9th in games started: 148.
He also started 7 playoff games (and pitched once in relief) for the Jays. He had a 3.79 ERA and a 2-4 record.
The last I saw, Gausman was talking about retirement, but he has said that he would consider coming back to the Jays. As I mentioned above, he was terrific the first time through the order, and far less good the second and third times. But I'm not sure that he would want to come back to pitch out of the pen.
The trade looks very good for the Jays, Brett Bateman was terrific for us, in his 41 games. Ty Southisene played well for 11 games with Vancouver, hitting .262/.380/.429. It will be interesting to watch how he does. FanGraphs had him listed as the Cubs 27th best prospect. He's fast and plays good defense in the middle of the infield.
It was great getting to watch Gausman pitch. The last five seasons wouldn't have been nearly as much fun without him.

item.content:encoded:
The Boston Red Sox should prioritize adding power to their lineup this offseason, but they may also need to fill a significant void in their starting rotation.
Veteran right-hander Sonny Gray is set to become a free agent after a sensational debut season with Boston. The soon-to-be 37-year-old led MLB with 18 wins while compiling a 2.72 ERA and 1.148 WHIP across 29 starts.
Gray was the Red Sox' de facto ace while Garrett Crochet missed most of the 2026 campaign due to injury. Without him, the projected 2027 rotation looks something like this:
- Garrett Crochet, LHP
- Payton Tolle, LHP
- Ranger Suarez, LHP
- Brayan Bello, RHP
- Jake Bennett, LHP
Not too shabby, but extremely left-handed-heavy. Plus, Bello was astoundingly bad as a starter this year with a 7.18 ERA over 11 outings.
So, who could potentially replace Gray in the Red Sox rotation next season? Here are a handful of intriguing right-handers expected to hit the open market this winter:
Michael King
- 2026 stats: 12-10, 3.21 ERA, 1.178 WHIP, 159 SO, 70 BB, 185 IP (32 starts with San Diego Padres)
- Age: 32
King bounced back from an injury-plagued 2025 with a stellar 2026 for San Diego. As a result, he'll likely be one of the pricier free-agent pitchers this offseason.
That shouldn't dissuade the Red Sox from pursuing the New England native and Boston College alum. King is as consistent as they come when healthy, and if he declines his $28 million option for 2027, he'd be an exceptional addition to the middle of Boston's already-strong rotation.
Kevin Gausman
- 2026 stats: 9-12, 4.51 ERA, 1.272 WHIP, 184 SO, 47 BB, 177.2 IP (23 starts with Toronto Blue Jays, nine starts with Chicago Cubs)
- Age: 36
Gausman is coming off a down season during which he was traded from Toronto to Chicago before the deadline. It was the first time since 2019 that the veteran finished a season with an ERA above 4.00.
That makes Gausman primed for a bounce-back campaign at 36 years old, just like Gray was upon being acquired from the St. Louis Cardinals last winter. Even if Gausman can't put up Cy Young-caliber numbers like Gray, he can be counted on to post. He has made at least 31 starts in each of his last six seasons.
Nick Martinez
- 2026 stats: 15-6, 3.10 ERA, 1.094 WHIP, 109 SO, 26 BB, 180 IP (31 starts with Tampa Bay Rays)
- Age: 36
After a rocky 2025 with Cincinnati, Martinez returned to form with a career year for the Rays. The nine-year veteran pitched exclusively as a starter for the first time in his career and blew away expectations while earning his first All-Star nod.
Martinez has a $20 million mutual option with the Rays for 2027, but mutual options are rarely picked up. He should be near the top of Boston's wish list if he's available.
Casey Mize
- 2026 stats: 6-10, 4.32 ERA, 1.226 WHIP, 110 SO, 38 BB, 131.1 IP (16 starts with Detroit Tigers, 10 starts with Padres)
- Age: 30
The 2026 season was a mixed bag for Mize. A first-time All-Star in 2025, he looked even better with the Tigers this year, posting a 2.70 ERA over 16 starts.
His strong start made him a valuable trade chip for Detroit, and he was shipped to the Padres for two prospects, including left-hander Kash Mayfield, San Diego's No. 2-ranked prospect.
Mize struggled mightily with the Padres, posting a 7.46 ERA in 10 starts. That raises obvious concerns as the former No. 1 overall draft pick enters free agency, but the upside he showed with Detroit makes him an intriguing option for the back end of Boston's rotation.
Freddy Peralta
- 2026 stats: 10-11, 4.42 ERA, 1.325 WHIP, 156 SO, 63 BB, 169 IP (22 starts with New York Mets, 10 starts with Rays)
- Age: 31
The former Milwaukee Brewers star struggled in Queens, but nothing really went right for the Mets in 2026. With the Rays, Peralta looked much more like his All-Star self, sporting a 3.25 ERA and 1.012 WHIP across 10 starts.
If you believe Peralta's midseason turnaround with Tampa wasn't a mirage, picking him as Gray's replacement is a no-brainer. His track record in his nine years in the league speaks for itself.

Pitching wins championships.
While that old adage still holds true, it has taken on a slightly different meaning in today's game, as teams need to successfully utilize their entire pitching staff to make a deep playoff run, rather than simply leaning on two or three starting pitchers to shoulder the load.
Still, a strong performance from the starting staff can give a team a major leg up. The Los Angeles Dodgers were the perfect example of that last October.
Ahead, we've ranked the playoff rotations of every postseason team. Which team's rotation is best positioned heading into the playoffs?
12. Houston Astros

Kevin Gausman's future with the Chicago Cubs could be an interesting storyline this offseason, but a return to Toronto may be more likely.
Cubs president of baseball operations Jed Hoyer has said he has wanted Gausman on his team for a long time. Chicago also pursued the veteran right-hander during his previous trip through free agency before finally acquiring him from the Blue Jays at the trade deadline.
Gausman, 35, finished the 2026 regular season with a 9-12 record, 4.51 ERA and 184 strikeouts over 177 2/3 innings in 32 starts between Toronto and Chicago. He posted a 1.27 WHIP.
After joining the Cubs, Gausman went 4-2 with a 4.83 ERA in nine starts. He struck out 57 and walked 11 over 50 1/3 innings while posting a 1.23 WHIP.
Mitch Bannon of The Athletic recently identified Gausman as a potential reunion candidate for Toronto.
“There’s also Kevin Gausman, who was traded by the Jays at the deadline and will enter free agency after the postseason," Bannon reported. "Like Springer and Scherzer, it’s unclear if Gausman’s playing days are over. If he returns, a reunion with Toronto seems likely.”
Gausman and his family developed strong ties to Toronto during his time with the organization, which could factor into his free-agent decision.
That could leave the Cubs with an interesting decision. Chicago has long liked Gausman and finally landed him this season, but the veteran could ultimately wind up back where he started the year.

item.content:encoded:
It didn't take long for free agent rumors to start swirling.
The Chicago Cubs were just swept by the San Diego Padres in the National League Wild Card Round a few days ago, and free-agent rumors are already circling the baseball world.
It will no doubt be a busy offseason for the Cubs, who have plenty of players hitting free agency. Players like Kevin Gausman, Shota Imanaga, David Peterson, and Carson Kelly will all test the open market this winter.
However, the biggest question mark this offseason for the Cubs is what they plan to do with their outfield. Both Ian Happ and Seiya Suzuki are free agents at the conclusion of this year's World Series. That leaves the team in a potential rough spot.
The Cubs have to answer one of these questions ahead of free agency:
- Do we bring back both Happ and Suzuki and simply run it back with the same outfield core?
- Do we pay Happ and let Suzuki walk, since he will cost much less?
- Do we pay Suzuki big money and let Happ walk because Suzuki gives us the best chance to win?
The front office will obviously weigh all these options ahead of free agency. However, it seems as if the Cubs have already made somewhat of a decision about Suzuki's future with the organization.
Patrick Mooney of The Athletic reported that "it's unlikely that the Cubs will get into a bidding war for Suzuki's services, let alone win one."
Hearing that the Cubs won't enter a bidding war for Suzuki doesn't bode well for their chances of getting him back. Teams like the Dodgers, Blue Jays, and Yankees are better suited to get into a bidding war for the slugger than the North Siders.
Mitch Bannon of the Athletic already reported that the Blue Jays will pursue Suzuki this offseason. Given that Toronto isn't afraid to spend on big-time players (e.g., Dylan Cease last offseason), there's a strong chance that the outfielder doesn't re-sign with the Cubs.
Losing Suzuki in free agency would be a big loss for the North Siders. He has been one of the team's best power hitters since the Cubs signed him out of Japan in 2022. The Japanese slugger has 113 home runs over his five MLB seasons and has 58 home runs with 189 RBI combined over the past two years.
The Cubs would be losing that power bat at the top of their lineup if he goes to another team. Unfortunately, it's very possible he does leave.

item.content:encoded:
SAN DIEGO — Was it a successful season in Wrigleyville?
It’s hard — even with baseball’s highest scoring lineup, best defense and best player — to judge 2026 as anything but a failure for the Cubs.
They set championship-level expectations and World Series goals.
Bowing out of the postseason after two games, their offense muzzled and MVP center fielder Pete Crow-Armstrong a non-factor, before the calendar even flipped to October?
They didn’t come close.
“The goal is to win, and we didn’t play well enough to do that,” third baseman Alex Bregman said. “It’s time to look in the mirror and get better.
“I know myself and a lot of these guys will be thinking about it every day of the offseason and let it fuel us. Just not good enough. We need to get better. In all areas.
“It starts now for everybody in this organization. Assess the year and come back and be better next year, because it wasn’t good enough.”
In the wake of such disappointment, there’s one overarching question: How does this not happen again?
It’s been back-to-back years of this, the Cubs dispatched by the rival Brewers in the NLDS a year ago. That was described as fuel for their fire this season, but the embers didn’t even burn long enough for a rematch.
Craig Counsell, whom the Cubs poached from those Brewers, has two early postseason exits in three seasons at the helm, with two years left on the contract that made him the game’s highest-paid skipper.
“We lost,” Counsell said. “There’s a response to it that we get to choose, and we’ve got to improve. Everybody can point at themselves and say, ‘We’ve got to get a little bit better.’
“We’re going to have to wait to accomplish the thing we really want to accomplish. … We didn’t finish it this year, and you hope that this has to be part of the journey to the ultimate prize.”
With the investments made in Counsell, Bregman, Crow-Armstrong and more, the expectations are not going to change. The Cubs will head into next season thinking World Series, just like this year.
But at least at the moment, they have a lot of questions to answer about how they’re going to get there.
What will make the 2027 group better equipped than the 2026 one?
That’s what the offseason — likely to be halted by a lengthy work stoppage — will teach us.
This was a roller-coaster campaign, with high highs and low lows, a lot of pitching injuries and a final-week downturn that came at exactly the wrong time.
The thoughts on the minds of everyone inside the losing clubhouse Wednesday were of further blows this team is about to take, the players who aren’t going to return, the pending free agents who were such a part of this group and its plan to deliver on those championship-level expectations.
“We’ll talk about the baseball plenty,” second baseman Nico Hoerner said, “but when you get through a locker room with people that you’re really close with and people that aren’t guaranteed to come back here — and not seeing this thing through the way a lot of us envisioned and believed in — that’s the stuff that doesn’t sit right and hurts.”
Perhaps most important for Jed Hoyer’s front office, the Cubs might have to replace their entire starting rotation, with lefties Matthew Boyd, Shota Imanaga and David Peterson, plus righties Clay Holmes and Kevin Gausman, all set to hit free agency.
Righties Cade Horton, Edward Cabrera and Ben Brown, plus lefty Justin Steele, make for an intriguing group of possible replacements, but all are coming off injuries, a risky play.
Then there’s the corner outfielders.
Right fielder Seiya Suzuki has been an offensive force it will be tough for the Cubs to replace; he’s expected to be one of the best hitters on the market and land a big contract.
Left fielder Ian Happ is a franchise fixture whose potential departure had teammates crying Wednesday night.
“He embodies the Cubs more than anyone I know,” shortstop Dansby Swanson said through tears.
Sentimentality is a rare reason to spend for baseball front offices. Happ didn’t have the type of offensive season he consistently has throughout his career though still played excellent defense and hit for power.
“All I can say is that I love being a Cub,” Happ said. “I’ve loved my time. I’ve loved the place, the people, Wrigley Field, the fan base. And it’s been truly special. I don’t think there’s a better place in baseball to play.”
With decisions to make, how Hoyer crafts his roster – and how these Cubs respond to another bout of playoff disappointment – will answer that overarching question, the only question that matters:
How do the Cubs make sure this doesn’t happen again?

What a way to sweep the Red Sox out of the playoffs! The Yankees brushed aside their inferior opponents, winning the two games by a combined score of 18-2. Every facet of their game was clicking — plate discipline, slug, bat-to-ball, two-strike hitting, situational hitting, base running, defense, and of course, starting pitching. It’s a winning recipe that leaves them in good stead for the upcoming ALDS date with Tampa.
The Yankees weren’t the only team to eliminate their opponents from the postseason on Wednesday so let’s jump straight into the action!
AL Wild Card Series Game 2
Chicago White Sox 7, Houston Astros 3
(Chicago wins 2-0)
After just two games, I can’t think of any playoff participant who wants to face these White Sox. That is a sentence that no one could conceive of typing at the start of the season. Two seasons removed from suffering the most losses in MLB history and on the back of three straight losing campaigns, this upstart Chicago squad came out of nowhere to crash the postseason, starting with a two game sweep of the Astros in their own building.
They have done so by scoring early and often, the White Sox lineup a deep unit one-thru-nine with multiple ways to hurt you. They work deep counts, foul pitches off, draw walks, and can put the ball in play, but can also slug the ball out of the yard from almost any spot in the batting order. On Tuesday, they scored three unanswered runs in the first two innings to put the Astros on the back foot from the word go, and Wednesday continued the trend with the Southsiders hanging a four-spot before the home team had a chance to bat.
They had a 1-0 lead just five pitches into the game against Astros ace Hunter Brown, Sam Antonacci leading off with a double before Kyle Teel drove him home with a single. A fielding error by Nick Allen on a Miguel Vargas grounder put a pair on, and three straight singles by Andrew Benintendi, Tristan Peters, and Chase Meidroth plated three more runs with help from a Lucas Spence throwing error from center.
Credit to the Astros, they did not roll over after going down four in the first and slowly chipped into the White Sox lead. Jeremy Peña led off the bottom of the first with a booming home run that clattered off the left field wall just below the train tracks. Cam Smith hit one to almost exactly the same spot with two outs in the second. Jose Altuve narrowly snuck a solo shot into the Crawford Boxes to lead off the fourth and just like that, a 4-0 game had become a 4-3 thriller.
An inning later it looked like the Astros would pull of the improbable and complete the comeback. Smith was hit by a pitch, Peña singled, and Isaac Paredes walked to load the bases with two outs for Altuve. However, reliever Anthony Kay got Altuve to fly out to medium right field to strand all three ducks on the pond. That left the door open for the White Sox to swing the momentum back in their own favor and they did so immediately. Benintendi and Peters drew a pair of walks to open the sixth, prompting Joe Espada to call on Bryan Abreu out of the bullpen. Astros owner Jim Crane vetoed a trade of Abreu to the Twins in the final minutes of the deadline, and Abreu rewarded that faith by hanging a 3-1 slider to Meidroth, the second baseman crushing a three-run bomb to left to put the final nail in the Astros’ coffin.
After sweeping this rematch of the 2005 World Series, the White Sox advance to the ALDS where they will face the AL Central champion Guardians, first pitch of Game 1 scheduled for 1:00 p.m. ET on Saturday.
NL Wild Card Series Game 2
Philadelphia Phillies 4, Atlanta Braves 3
(Series tied 1-1)
The Phillies’ season was hanging by a thread until some late heroics by Kyle Schwarber, Bryce Harper, and Alec Bohm sent this thrilling series to a decisive Game 3. It was a pitchers’ duel early between two starters trending in opposite directions. Tyler Mahle entered his first career playoff start with a sub-two ERA after joining the Braves from the Giants at the deadline while Cristopher Sánchez posted an ERA above five in the month of September (though will still likely wrap up his second straight runner-up finish in NL Cy Young balloting).
The one thing the two starters do have in common is first inning struggles and that certainly played out in this game. Mahle allowed a leadoff double to Trea Turner and consecutive one-out singles by Bryce Harper and Alex Bohm to allow the Phillies to jump ahead, 1-0. However, Sánchez issued a leadoff walk to Ronald Acuña Jr., who promptly stole second and scored the tying run on a Matt Olson single.
Both starters settled in from there, trading zeroes for the next five innings, until things unraveled for Sánchez and his defense in the seventh. Sean Murphy worked a leadoff walk and Ha-Seong Kim reached on a bunt single to put a pair on with no outs. Drake Baldwin then clubbed what looked like a routine liner to right, but Harper misplayed it horrifically breaking in on the ball only to watch it sail over his glove and to the wall for what was ruled as an RBI double. Sánchez intentionally walked Ozzie Albies to load the bases, and Olson made him pay with a sac fly to double the Braves lead, 3-1.
What should have been a hammer blow to the Phillies morale did not play out as such. Schwarber immediately responded with a towering leadoff shot off lefty reliever Dylan Lee, and Harper atoned for his misplay by going back-to-back to retie the game, 3-3. That sent this game to extra innings, where the much-maligned Alec Bohm continued his redemption tour. Bohm was on the bubble of being non-tendered during the offseason, but the Phillies kept him around and drove in the first run of the series with an RBI double in the first inning of Game 1. The third baseman was the ultimate hero in this one, his opposite field solo homer off rookie Didier Fuentes in the 10th to keep the Phillies season alive and force a decisive Game 3.
San Diego Padres 4, Chicago Cubs 1
(San Diego wins 2-0)
This game featured surprisingly quick hooks of both starters as neither manager wanted to risk leaving their highest leverage relievers unused. One was certainly more deserved than the other, Kevin Gausman allowing three runs on five hits in 3.1 innings. The Cubs were desperate for starting pitching at the Trade Deadline and Gausman was supposed to be their big prize. However, he flopped after making the move from the Blue Jays, pitching to a 4.83 ERA in nine starts post-deadline, and his stinker tonight was the beginning of the end of the Cubs’ season. Nick Pivetta on the other hand held Chicago to a run on three hits and two walks with four strikeouts in 3.1 innings, but Craig Stammen seemed determined to play the matchups in this one.
Ty France got things started with a double to lead off the second, advancing to third on a Jackson Merrill single, who then stole second to put a pair in scoring position for Xander Bogaerts. The veteran shortstop opened the scoring with an RBI single, which brought Ethan Salas to the plate. The 20-year-old became the youngest catcher ever to appear in a playoff game, and in his first postseason PA, he lifted a sac fly to center to plate Merrill as the Padres’ second run.
The real story of this series has been the Cubs’ inability to score. They led MLB scoring 5.25 runs per game, spearheaded by shoo-in NL MVP Pete Crow-Armstrong and his MLB-leading 45 home runs (PCA would go 0-for-7 with four strikeouts in the series). They found themselves shut out through the first 12.1 innings of this series, finally breaking the seal in the fourth on a Seiya Suzuki single, Ian Happ walk, and Nico Hoerner RBI single. A Carson Kelly hit-by-pitch loaded the bases with two outs, but Dansby Swanson flew out to stand all three in place.
San Diego immediately punished them for failing to fully cash in on that scoring opportunity. Bogaerts reached on a one-out double, prompting Craig Counsell to call on Daniel Palencia in relief of Gausman. Palencia yanked a 101 mph fastball right into Sheets’ nitro zone down and in, and the lefty crushed it to right for a mammoth two-run blast.
It was all hands on deck from there from the Padres bullpen looking to protect their lead for the final five innings of the contest. They proved how terrifying a relief corps they’ve been all season, allowing just three base runners — a Michael Busch walk with two outs in the fifth, a Tyrone Taylor pinch-hit single with one out in the eighth, and a Hoerner one-out double off Mason Miller in the ninth — after the Cubs stranded the bases loaded to end the fourth.
San Diego advances to the NLDS where they will face the best team in baseball. It’s an unenviable position to come up against presumptive NL Cy Young Jacob Misiorowski and the 103-win Brewers. Game 1 of that series is scheduled for October 3rd with first pitch time contingent upon the result of Game 3 between Philly and Atlanta.

30 de septiembre de 2026 Hora: 15:43
Padres de San Diego defendió con autoridad su feudo en el primer encuentro de la Serie del Comodín de la Liga Nacional, tras imponerse con una contundente blanqueada de 8-0 sobre Cachorros de Chicago en el Petco Park. La novena californiana cimentó su victoria gracias a una electrizante exhibición ofensiva liderada por Fernando Tatis Jr. y una sobresaliente apertura del derecho Michael King.
El ataque de los frailes no se hizo esperar y castigó temprano al abridor de Chicago, Matthew Boyd. En la conclusión del primer episodio, el poder dominicano se hizo sentir en todo el estadio: Tatis Jr. inauguró la pizarra al depositar la esférica en las gradas del jardín central, seguido por otro cuadrangular de Manny Machado entre los prados izquierdo y derecho. La ofensiva continuó en el tercer capítulo, cuando el antesalista conectó un doblete contra la barda que bañó al jardinero Pete Crow-Armstrong para remolcar a su compatriota y ampliar la ventaja a 3-0.
El arubeño Xander Bogaerts se unió al festín ofensivo contra el zurdo de Cachorros, despachando un dantesco cuadrangular solitario que aterrizó en las gradas del jardín izquierdo. El asedio de San Diego se profundizó en la quinta entrada, cuando Jackson Merrill conectó un sencillo remolcador de dos anotaciones que puso el marcador 6-0. En ese mismo episodio, Ty France pisó la registradora para sumar la séptima rayita del encuentro, aprovechando un pasbol del receptor Carson Kelly.
Más allá de la demostración de poder, Fernando Tatis Jr. demostró otra de las herramientas de su repertorio: la velocidad en las almohadillas. El jardinero causó estragos en la defensiva visitante al estafarse la intermedia y, apoyado en un errático tiro de Kelly hacia la segunda base, completó una fantástica y agresiva carrera hasta el plato para sellar el 8 – 0 definitivo.
Desde el montículo, Michael King maniató por completo a los maderos rivales. El diestro se adjudicó la victoria tras lanzar siete entradas en blanco, en las que apenas toleró un indiscutible, otorgó tres pasaportes y retiró a ocho bateadores por la vía del ponche.
LEA TAMBIÉN:
La serie al mejor de tres compromisos continuará esta noche a las 10:00 p.m., cuando ambas novenas vuelvan a saltar al diamante. Para este duelo crucial, Cachorros de Chicago dependerá de los envíos del derecho Kevin Gausman, quien subirá a la lomita con la obligación de evitar la eliminación. Por su parte, Padres de San Diego le entregarán la esférica a Nick Pivetta, quien tendrá la misión de definir la serie y sellar el pase a la Serie Divisional.

item.content:encoded:
Pete Crow-Armstrong's historic season just produced another staggering number, this time away from the baseball field.
The Chicago Cubs star's one-of-one 2024 Topps Chrome Update MLB Debut Patch Autograph sold for $1.098 million at Goldin.
The PSA Gem Mint 10 card, which also received a PSA 10 autograph grade, features the MLB Debut patch from Crow-Armstrong's first major-league game on September 11, 2023.
It is a massive sale by itself.
The timing makes it even more striking.
Crow-Armstrong just completed a historic 40-home run, 40-stolen base season and helped Chicago reach the postseason. Now, only days later, his signature rookie card has approached the MLB Debut Patch record while Crow-Armstrong and the Cubs enter an elimination game against the San Diego Padres.
$1,098,000: Winning bid for Pete Crow-Armstrong’s debut patch jersey tonight at @GoldinCo.
PCA’s 2024 rookie salary: $740,000. pic.twitter.com/d21WopsNpx
— Darren Rovell (@darrenrovell) September 30, 2026
Pete Crow-Armstrong Card Sells for $1.098 Million
Crow-Armstrong's card was one of the most significant MLB Debut Patch cards to reach the market since Paul Skenes' one-of-one sold in 2025.
Goldin listed the card as Crow-Armstrong's 2024 Topps Chrome Update MLB Debut Patch Autograph 1/1, graded PSA Gem Mint 10 with a PSA/DNA Gem Mint 10 autograph grade.
The $1.098 million result also produced a remarkable comparison highlighted by Rovell.
Crow-Armstrong earned roughly $740,000 during the 2024 season, meaning a collector just paid considerably more for his one-of-one rookie card than the Cubs paid Crow-Armstrong to play an entire major-league season.
But the final auction price may be even more notable for what it narrowly failed to accomplish.
Pete Crow-Armstrong Falls $12,000 Short of Paul Skenes Record
Crow-Armstrong came extraordinarily close to taking down the benchmark for MLB Debut Patch cards.
Skenes' one-of-one 2024 Topps Chrome Update MLB Debut Patch Autograph sold for $1.11 million through Fanatics Collect in March 2025. The price included the buyer's premium and established the Skenes card as the highest-selling MLB Debut Patch at the time.
Crow-Armstrong finished at $1.098 million.
The difference?
Just $12,000.
That puts Crow-Armstrong and Skenes in remarkably similar territory despite playing dramatically different positions and arriving in the majors with different levels of prospect hype.
Skenes was the No. 1 overall pick in the 2023 MLB Draft and won National League Rookie of the Year in his first season. His Debut Patch became a national story even before it surfaced, with the Pittsburgh Pirates famously offering the young collector who pulled it a package that included 30 years of season tickets.
Crow-Armstrong's card reached seven figures after a different catalyst: one of the greatest individual seasons ever produced by a Cubs player.
Pete Crow-Armstrong Made Cubs History Before $1.1 Million Sale
The auction could hardly have closed at a better moment for Crow-Armstrong's hobby profile.
On September 24, Crow-Armstrong stole his 40th base of the season, joining the exclusive 40-40 club after already reaching 45 home runs.
He became just the seventh player in MLB history to record at least 40 homers and 40 stolen bases in the same season. He also became the first Cubs player to accomplish the feat.
And he did it on the same night Chicago clinched an NL Wild Card berth with a 2-1 victory over the Miami Marlins.
Crow-Armstrong entered the postseason hitting .280 with 45 home runs and 107 RBIs while appearing in all 159 Cubs games through the clinching victory.
That transformed the timing of the Goldin auction.
Collectors were not merely bidding on the Debut Patch of a promising young Cubs player.
They were bidding on the Debut Patch of a 24-year-old who had just completed the first 40-40 season in franchise history.
Now the attention shifts back to what Crow-Armstrong can do on the field.
Cubs Face Elimination Against Padres After 8-0 Loss
Chicago enters Game 2 of its Wild Card Series against San Diego needing a victory to keep its season alive.
The Padres routed the Cubs 8-0 in Game 1 on September 29.
San Diego starter Michael King took a no-hit bid into the seventh inning and ultimately allowed only one hit over seven scoreless frames while striking out eight. Fernando Tatis Jr., Manny Machado and Xander Bogaerts each homered for the Padres.
The Cubs will send Kevin Gausman to the mound for Game 2 opposite Nick Pivetta
There is at least one reason for optimism surrounding Crow-Armstrong specifically.
Chicago dominated San Diego during the regular season, winning five of six games and outscoring the Padres 55-28.
Crow-Armstrong was one of the Cubs' biggest problems for San Diego.
He hit .364 with four home runs in the six regular-season meetings.
Chicago will need another performance like that now.
Crow-Armstrong has already produced one of the defining baseball-card sales of 2026 and one of the most statistically significant seasons in Cubs history.
Whether his week is remembered primarily for a $1.098 million card sale or for what happens in October now depends on what Crow-Armstrong and the Cubs do next.

item.content:encoded:
The San Diego Padres blitzed the Chicago Cubs in Game 1 of the NL Wild Card series, 8-0, to put themselves one win away from a date with the Milwaukee Brewers in the NLDS. Plenty of Padres deserve credit for Tuesday night's dominant performance, but none more than soon-to-be-free agent Michael King.
San Diego's ace put together one of the best postseason starts in recent memory, carrying a no-hitter into the seventh inning. He finished with seven scoreless frames, allowing one hit, three walks and recording eight strikeouts. As Padres fans celebrate King's masterclass, prospective free agency suitors are chomping at the bit. Here are a few potential landing spots:
Atlanta Braves
The Braves rotation is a bit scarce behind Chris Sale. Tyler Mahle has eviscerated the competition since arriving at the trade deadline, but he's a free agent next winter. AJ Smith-Shawver, J.R. Ritchie and Owen Murphy are all exciting young arms, but it's unclear which of them will click as full-time starters — and how soon. Martín Pérez, one of this season's great surprises for Atlanta, is also an upcoming free agent.
Atlanta doesn't typically pay sticker price on free agent pitchers but there is immense pressure to compete now — right now — in the twilight years of Sale's career. He won't be able to anchor this rotation forever and the Braves need to start hedging their bets, just in case Father Time catches up.
King, with a 3.21 ERA and 1.18 WHIP, has made 32 starts and pitched a career-high 185 innings this season. The Braves need depth and dependability most desperately, and that's something King can provide. It doesn't hurt that he is building a nice postseason résumé for himself.
Baltimore Orioles
Every winter, we all wonder if Baltimore might finally upgrade its pitching staff. The Corbin Burnes era burned bright and fast. Shane Baz was a savvy trade addition last winter, but the Orioles still struggled to field five quality, healthy starters for the 162-game duration of the regular season.
Trevor Rogers, their best pitcher two years running, will now enter free agency. That leaves Baltimore's front office will a clear and immediate need in the rotation. It seems like the O's new ownership group will, on some level, spend more than the previous administration. The Pete Alonso signing was a stark departure from business as usual in Baltimore. As such, it's not hard to envision the O's ponying up for a second-tier ace like Michael King; the Tarik Skubals of the world are still outside their price range, no doubt.
If Kyle Bradish can finally get healthy for a year, and if the O's deign to re-sign Rogers (or pursue another mid-rotation arm in addition to King), this rotation could shape up quite nicely. Baltimore has the offensive firepower to compete in the AL East. King can help round out a postseason-caliber roster.
Toronto Blue Jays
A nightmare Blue Jays season has finally come to an end, but Toronto should be right back in the postseason fray next season with better luck and an productive winter. The Jays front office is probably the most aggressive in baseball outside of L.A. or New York.
Last offseason, their big fish was Dylan Cease, who immediately turned in a Cy Young-caliber campaign. At the trade deadline, Toronto did not strictly sell, despite sitting near the bottom of the standings. The Jays went out and added José Soriano, another frontline starter at the peak of his powers.
Toronto can expect a healtheir Trey Yesavage in 2027, too, so a premium free agent addition (like King) could quickly transform the Blue Jays rotation into one of the deepest and most fearsome in the American League. If Vladimir Guerrero Jr. and Toronto's boppers put their best foot forward, there's no reason Toronto can't win the division and compete (again) for a World Series.
Houston Astros
The Astros went bullpen against bullpen in their AL Wild Card series opener against the White Sox. Houston was lucky Chicago only managed six runs, with many, many base-runners stranded in scoring position. That did not mean much for the Astros, unfortunately, as the Chicago bullpen — against all odds — mostly kept a more seasoned Houston lineup in check.
Houston has a proper 1A ace in Hunter Brown, but the rotation behind him is total patchwork. Peter Lambert put together a solid campaign and Ethan Pecko faired well in his first taste of MLB action, but the Astros can't really trust anyone besides Brown. Tatsuya Imai, their prized free agent addition last winter, was little more than a bulk reliever in his rookie season.
The Astros have gotten cheaper and cheaper in recent years and the results are getting worse and worse, predictably. Still, this core has competed for a World Series in the not-so-distant past, and we know ownership is capable of spending at the upper echelon of free agency. King would do a lot to solidify the Astros' pitching plans in 2027.
Chicago Cubs
Injuries decimated the Cubs rotation this season. Justin Steele, Cade Horton and Ben Brown should all return in 2027, which is a major, natural influx of talent. If Edward Cabrera can rebound, the Cubs rotation will be all rainbows and sunshine — at least on paper.
But as this season once again reminded us, what happens "on paper" almost never translates to reality. Shōta Imanaga and Matthew Boyd are both upcoming free agents. Kevin Gausman and Clay Holmes, Chicago's emergency deadline rentals, are also halfway out the door. There's uncertainty around how exactly the likes of Steele and Horton will perform coming off of major elbow surgeries, too. So the Cubs should play it safe and hyper-focus on pitching depth.
The rotation could be what sends Chicago home against San Diego. So, why not use the Padres own weapons against them in free agency and sign King? "Stability" is a word that comes to mind with King, and that's exactly what the Cubs need right now.

item.content:encoded:
starting pitcher Kevin Gausman revealed his honest thoughts about the Toronto Blue Jays trading him at the MLB trade deadline.
Gausman, who starts for the Cubs on Wednesday against the San Diego Padres in a must-win game in the MLB Wild Card round, was dealt from Toronto to Chicago at the deadline for Brett Bateman and Ty Southisene.
According to the veteran hurler, the trade surprised him, as a conversation with Blue Jays GM Ross Atkins led him to believe he wasn't going to be dealt.
Kevin Gausman Shares Honest Thoughts on Blue Jays Trade
Speaking on the "Baseball Isn't Boring" podcast, Gausman shared his honest thoughts about the trade sending him from "The Six" to "The Windy City" at the deadline.
"We kind of had some conversations a couple days leading up that there was some interest. But (the Jays) didn't feel like it was going to get to a point where they thought they were going to get what they wanted to trade me," Gausman said (via Toronto Sun).
"They picked up a starter (Jameson Taillon) and (I thought), 'OK, probably going to lose a starter.' I didn't think it was going to be me, to be honest. But this game is crazy and you never know what's going to happen."
Cubs Need Kevin Gausman to Pitch Like An Ace in Playoffs
After dropping Game 1 of a possible three-game Wild Card series against San Diego by a score of 8-0, the Cubs are in a must-win situation on Wednesday when Gausman takes the mound against Nick Pivetta and the Padres.
With the Cubs following the trade, Gausman was 4-2 with a 4.83 ERA in nine starts for Chicago. He wasn't exactly what the team was hoping for, but if he can put up a great start for Chicago against San Diego and help the team force a deciding Game 3 in the Wild Card round, then it will make the trade look a lot better for the Cubs.
A free agent following this season, Gausman could potentially look to make a reunion in Toronto if he decides to pitch again.
He admitted on the podcast that being traded away from Toronto was so tough for him and his family as they all loved living and playing north of the border.
"I had been in Toronto for so long and so comfortable with the organization, it was my second home. We had a home. It was hard to leave, to be honest. A lot of great moments, not so great moments and (this) year was a really tough year to be a part of. The hardest part was the family aspect. My kids having to go to a new family room and trying to make friends in a short period of time. That was probably the hardest part, seeing how much it affected my wife and kids. They got comfortable just like I did," Gausman said.
We'll see what the future holds for Gausman, but right now, his focus is on winning Game 2 for the Cubs against the Padres.

Fernando Tatis Jr. Talks Padres' Dominant MLB Playoffs G1 Win vs. Cubs, 'Beautiful Baseball Night'
Fernando Tatís Jr. reflected on what was essentially a perfect night for the San Diego Padres on Tuesday, as they cruised to an 8-0 win over the Chicago Cubs in Game 1 of their National League Wild Card Series.
Speaking to reporters following the one-sided victory, Tatís said, "We couldn't have scripted it any better than what happened tonight. Today was a beautiful baseball night for every San Diegan."
Playing in front of over 47,000 fans at Petco Park in San Diego, the Padres poured it on from the get-go, as they led 2-0 after one inning and 7-0 through five.
Tatís was a big part of the Padres' offensive success in Game 1, as he launched a solo home run to lead off the bottom of the first inning.
All told, Tatís went 2-for-3, walked once, stole a base and scored three runs to go along with the one homer and one RBI.
Veteran third baseman Manny Machado also homered and drove in a pair, while starting pitcher Michael King authored a masterpiece, allowing one hit and no runs, while walking three and striking out eight over seven innings.
King and the San Diego pitching staff notably shut down Cubs outfielder and NL MVP front-runner Pete Crow-Armstrong, as he went 0-for-3 with three strikeouts and one walk.
The Padres are now just one win away from advancing to the National League Division Series for the second time in the past three seasons.
They will send Nick Pivetta to the mound for Wednesday night's Game 2 of the NLWCS, while Chicago will counter with Kevin Gausman.

On Tuesday, the Chicago Cubs and San Diego Padres will open up their playoff series in California.
The Cubs finished up the regular season on Sunday when they beat the Boston Red Sox by a score of 6-2.
Chicago Cubs Announce Dansby Swanson Decision
For Tuesday’s game, the Cubs have announced their starting lineup.
Underdog MLB wrote: “Cubs 9/29 P. Crow-Armstrong CF A. Bregman DH M. Busch 1B S. Suzuki RF I. Happ LF N. Hoerner 2B P. Ramírez 3B C. Kelly C D. Swanson SS M. Boyd SP”
Dansby Swanson will open up the series hitting 9th in the order.
The 2021 World Series Champion is in the middle of his fourth year with the Cubs.
He finished the regular season batting .213 with 91 hits, 19 home runs, 69 RBIs, 82 runs and 17 stolen bases in 126 games.
Swanson was the top pick in the 2015 MLB Draft out of Vanderbilt.
He spent the first seven years of his career with the Atlanta Braves.
The two-time All-Star will turn 33 in February.
